#Question 10
#Single bracket return a smaller list. Double brackets extract the actual element from the list.
#Questioon 11
#R makes this distinction because a list can contain different types of objects, strings, numbers, vectors, and logical values. Single bracket select elements while keeping them in the list. Double brackets extract the actual object.
```{r}
#Part E
inventory <- list(item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"),price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00), in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))
print(inventory$item[inventory$in_stock])

inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
inventory
```
#Question 12
#inventory$item[inventory$in_stock] works cause the item and in_stock vectors have corresponding positions in the list. The logical vector contains TRUE, TRUE, FALSE so R selects the items at position where the value is TRUE. Therefore it returns "Notebook" and "Pen" while excluding "Eraser".
#Question 13
#Using three seperate vectors can cause mistakes if items are added, removed, or recorded in only one vector. Grouping related vector in a list makes the data easier to organize and access.

#Conclusion
#Vectors store elements of the same basic type, while list can store different types of objects, including vectors and other lists. Vector are useful for storing and processing similar values, such as prices and grades. Lists are useful for grouping related objeccts thta may have different types. For tabular data, such as an inventory with item names, prices, and stock statuses, a data frame is often the best choice.
